speaker: Megan Palmer
words: Today I'm here speaking with Christina Tramack on December 4th, 2025 for the Everyday Harmony Oral History Project. That's a project where I'm talking to everyday barbershoppers about their experience with the style, community, and culture of barbershop music. Christina has officially been a barbershopper since they were just 10 years old and has had nothing short of, like, a pretty awesome barbershop journey since then. And I can't wait to get to talk to you about it. Thanks so much for having me here in the Tramack home.

speaker: Christina Tramack
words: Thanks for coming up and being here.

speaker: Megan
words: Thank you. So, for most people I might ask a question, like, "How did you first get involved in barbershop?" But that seems like kind of a silly question for you. So I would love to kick this off by asking a question, like, literally close to home: What role did barbershop play in your childhood and in your family?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah, so barbershop has always been around in my life. I was born into it quite literally. My parents met through barbershop. They were both — they are both barbershop brats, actually, and then they met at a show and then got married and had kids and all, we all grew up around barbershop. So it's just been part of the family since our beginnings.

speaker: Megan
words: Literally generations, right?

speaker: Christina
words: Literally.

speaker: Megan
words: You're like the third generation on one side?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah, I'm third on my mom's. My mom's mom started in Harmony Inc. the year they began in 1959. So she would — she would claim she was not a charter member, but she was. She joined before the year was up. And my dad, on his line, I'm a fifth generation barbershopper. So it goes back to my great-great-grandfather. Yeah, that's how that works.

speaker: Megan
words: That's so awesome. Do you have like any especially early memories of barbershop, like being around or like being a part of your life?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah, I have a couple memories of just even in the house... If we can — let's move you just for now, there we go. So childhood, I remember my parents having quartet rehearsals at the house, so we were always "music center"; people would always come to us. We would host parties as well, but they would have quartet rehearsals as well. And I have one specific memory of when a quartet, you know, is standing facing each other in that "bucket" or "circle," whatever you call it.

speaker: Megan
words: In the "box."

speaker: Christina
words: The box, so many names for it. When I was a kid — little, little — I can't even tell you how old, I would crawl into the middle of the pit, of the circle there and look up at the people singing. And I did that for both my mom and dad's quartet, but I distinctly remember my mom's quartet and just like, just being surrounded by the harmony and lookin' up and enjoying it, yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: Were you also a part of music like at your school, like in addition to barbershop?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah. I wanted to be in band when I started middle school, but at the time we had to pick band or chorus. They don't have that anymore, but — that restriction — but I was influenced to start in chorus, and that was around the same time I joined barbershop for the first time too. So like all the choral stuff happened all at once.

speaker: Megan
words: So you joined your first chorus at how old?

speaker: Christina
words: I was 10 when I joined them.

speaker: Megan
words: Okay. And tell me about that experience.

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah. My mom has been the director [of New England Voices in Harmony] for a long time now. She didn't start as co-director, but she was pretty close to co-director at their formation. They started in 2000, chartered in 2001 with Harmony Inc. I joined in 2004.

speaker: Megan
words: And that's New England Voices in Harmony, right?

speaker: Christina
words: That's New England Voices in Harmony. And it's — so I joined fairly early on in their, like, just development as a chorus. I did not pass my first audition. [laughs]

speaker: Megan
words: Dang. The secrets come out

speaker: Christina
words: And so…

speaker: Megan
words: Because you were, what? Ten!

speaker: Christina
words: I was ten!

speaker: Megan
words: Okay.

speaker: Christina
words: And at the time we could pick our own song. Now we sing the theme song and that's just the standard for everyone coming in. But we could pick our own song, so I sang "Under the Boardwalk," and I was a lead. And I guess I got lost too many times without coming back. I mean, it was a quartet, you know, audition, so it's tough as a ten year old. I remember crying in the bathroom after that and just sobbing. Just so sad. My mom tried to encourage me, and I was just like, "I can't believe it!" But I did pass the second time I tried it, and I've been a member ever since. I took a short break while I was in college cause I was in Tennessee, but other than that I've been active with them and singing for 21 years now.

speaker: Megan
words: Now, with your mom being the director of the chorus and your dad being involved in barbershop, when would you say you like realized that your parents were like "kind of a big deal" in this space?

speaker: Christina
words: [laughs, pushes cat away] Just push him off. [sighs] I would probably pin it around the time I joined in all honesty. I was obviously aware of barbershop and like the influence it had on us and our lives, but until I was really in it, I didn't really know how big of a deal they were. And like, my dad was the director of the Nashua Granite Statesmen at the time. And in those days, it was about the peak of where that chorus was. They were consistently averaging "A," they were really, you know, just a phenomenal chorus, and my dad was the frontline director during that whole time, which is awesome. And then my — again, my mom's been directing the chorus as well. So their influences grew since then too. But like, even then it was like, "Okay, this is kind of a big deal." Yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: Did you ever feel any, like, pressure because of that? Like, was there ever a world in which you didn't sing barbershop? Like, would that have been okay?

speaker: Christina
words: [laughs] So, yeah, definitely felt pressure, but not in, like, needing to sing. I don't think they really forced us, although my mom did drag me to a lot of rehearsals before I was ten. When she would coach or she would go — she was directing other choruses at the time — and she would just kind of drag me along to see if this one would stick. And New England voices did; there were younger people in the chorus, so that was really the big draw there. But the — oh gosh, I lost my train of thought here.

speaker: Megan
words: Joining the chorus, feeling pressure. Yeah.

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah. It was more so walking through conventions and feeling the pressure of like, "Wow, everyone knows my dad."

speaker: Megan
words: Mm-hmm.

speaker: Christina
words: And being introduced to everyone as "Steve Tramack's daughter." And that was just like the constant. And I would get recognized later on because of that too. And that's the part that felt more like pressure instead of the actual getting involved in singing, cause it's just, it's intimidating when your parents are well known.

speaker: Megan
words: Even in such a niche hobby.

speaker: Christina
words: Right.

speaker: Megan
words: It still feels like they're rock stars sometimes.

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah. Absolutely. When you're in that bubble, absolutely.

speaker: Megan
words: Now you've sung with New England Voices in Harmony now for over 20 years minus, you know, that like one break you took for college. Can you tell me a little bit about that journey? Any particular high points for the chorus or for you as a chorus singer?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah. I've gotten most, if not all, of my vocal training through the chorus since I joined. I've had coachings with quartets at that by now too, but all of my upbringing vocally, I've never seen like a vocal coach. Yeah. Like I mean — and I was in chorus in school, so I did get training there too, but it's just, barbershop's different.

speaker: Megan
words: Yes.

speaker: Christina
words: And I've been on the journey with this chorus. When we joined — when I joined, we were not a medalist chorus at International. We became one in 2006, which is super cool. At the time they were doing placements one through four, not one through five for medals, and we were fourth place that year. And I still remember my mom just bawling on the phone with my dad cause he wasn't at that convention when we — it was in Jacksonville, Florida. That was a very, very cool moment.

speaker: Megan
words: Had you sung at the international contest before up to that point and like not medaled or was that the first time being there?

speaker: Christina
words: My first international was '05, and we did not medal, but we were in the top 10, and there's only one round for choruses, so that was cool. I think we were at sixth place that year, if I remember correctly. But yeah, that first medal in '06 was incredible. And then, fast forward to 2014, we won the International Contest for the first time, which was just mind blowing. I think we won by one total point. It was a very, very close contest.

speaker: Megan
words: Awesome.

speaker: Christina
words: We basically tied with second place, and we said we would share our medals with them. Absolutely. But it was a very, very close contest. That same contest, one of our chapter quartets also won the quartet contest. So that was a really fun and cool year of like— our reigning year of having both the reigning champion quartet as part of the reigning championship chorus was a lot for that quartet.

speaker: Megan
words: So cool.

speaker: Christina
words: But it was, yeah, it was very, very cool. And then we also won in 2018, and that one came out of nowhere. We were not expecting to win that one. It just... "right place at right time." And even recently last month, we had our International. It's always in November, at the beginning of November. And a lifelong goal of my mom's as director, but also in her own personal life, has been to score like average "A." And we did that for the first time this past November. We got an 81.5 and we're very, very happy about it. And we got second place, and it's the most proud second place medal we've ever received.

speaker: Megan
words: Sometimes second place feels just as good at first when you know you worked so dang hard for it.

speaker: Christina
words: It was the goal that we wanted, and it's the goal that we achieved. And it's been years and years in the making. So some really, really cool points for the chorus there.

speaker: Megan
words: Yeah, getting to see a chorus develop like that... Would you say anything, like, changed in the way that you were thinking or rehearsing or practicing? Like, what in your opinion has, like, been the thing that's allowed the chorus to, like, you know, ascend and, like, achieve so much?

speaker: Christina
words: I think it's part the culture which has changed a lot actually over the years. And the members themselves, we've had a lot of change over. There's a few of us that are still hanging on for, for a while now. We can shove him off if he's…

speaker: Megan
words: [talking to cat] Do you need to be there? [both laugh] You'd be fine if you weren't playing with the microphone!

speaker: Christina
words: He just is playing with the wrong things. [laughs] Yeah, so the culture has shifted, the members have shifted. Even recently we've gained a bunch of new members, and it's even shifted again in recent, recent times. So I think that's helped with the…

speaker: Megan
words: You were being good until you was being bad.

speaker: Christina
words: You were. You can come over here. You don't have to play with that. Or you can go down. There we go. [laughs]

speaker: Megan
words: It's part of the "everyday harmony" It's…

speaker: Christina
words: That's it.

speaker: Megan
words: It's praxis. [both laugh]

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah, so I would say it comes down to the motivation of the individual people that's helped us grow and learn and all be on the same page and share the same goals of what we want to accomplish.

speaker: Megan
words: And you mentioned about the culture, like, kind of shifting. Like, how would you describe the culture of New England Voices? What makes it special?

speaker: Christina
words: It is very unique right now. As I, yeah, as I was saying, it was... we had some tough times just after COVID. COVID, we were still active, we did Zoom. We, like most choruses, we tried something virtual. And we made it through, and it was fine, but it was definitely like a pullback of, like, reassessing where we want to be as a chorus. And then the year, like, I want to say '22, '23, around those years, even as recent as last year, there's just been a lot of burnout on the older members, myself included. I'm one of the oldest members there now as far as longevity of being there. And I was really feeling the burnout last year of just... it was a drag to get to rehearsals, just cause it was — we felt stuck and like, there wasn't any like movement forward.

speaker: Christina
words: And then this new shift of people came in, and it's really sparked a new drive and energy in the chorus. And now that we — our retreat weekends are really special where, especially for offsite, we do them early fall, like usually September. It's a time to integrate and to really like bond with our chorusmates, especially when we're offsite, and we've been going to Rolling Ridge in Massachusetts. It's a really beautiful, like retreat destination, quite literally. It's an old house that's made for retreats for groups. And we've done that the last two years, and it's been really cool to like, to be offsite again, cause we would do our retreat weekends at home base in Nashua at our regular rehearsal hall, and it's fine, but there's no game time afterwards. There's no way for us to all bond. So I think with that, the new people have integrated, and it's just been a new kind of buzzing energy of like, "We're really excited to perform and excel and be excited about growing as a chorus and yay we made the "A" score. Let's see what we can do next." So, yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: It's really cool to be able to make it through a tough time as a group, to come out the other side of it and to just be something new and also the same.

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: So it's really cool. Now in addition to singing in a chorus, you've also sung in quite a few quartets. What was the first quartet you sang in and what was that experience like?

speaker: Christina
words: My first quartet was Cloud Nine, which I still love that name. Took us forever to find that name. I'm actually currently singing with that lead only we've swapped parts. I'm singing lead now, and she's singing baritone in our current quartet High Gear. But Cloud Nine was made up of myself on baritone and I was a teenager, I was in high school. And Jean Kroll, who was a Harmony Queen with Synchronicity in 2004 by that point. I think we formed in like '09, I want to say. And then Kate Steer was our tenor, who was another member of the chorus. She was a baritone at the time, so she swapped parts to be part of this quartet. And then Jen Selby was the lead.

speaker: Christina
words: And we made the top 10 our first year, which is amazing. We jumped a huge amount in score from area to IC&C that year. Cause we'd like just barely formed, and then we went to area, and we just barely qualified with like a 64-5 or something like that. And then we made it to International. It was like a 72 that we got. And it was — we got novice awards for those years. And then fast forwarding to 2011, yeah, it was 2011, we medaled for the first time. We got fifth place, which was super, super cool. But we ended up having to call it from there. Cause I was in college that year, and they were having a really hard time even those first few months doing a long distance kind of quartet, even if it was just the baritone. So...

speaker: Megan
words: It changes things though.

speaker: Christina
words: It does. It does. And I mean, I'm experiencing that now. Our bass in high gear, Dev Green is a snowbird, so she's down in Florida for half of the year, basically, she's down there now. So we're a trio until she returns. But yeah, Cloud Nine was super fun. And then they asked if they could continue with a different baritone and change their name. And the baritone even called me and was like, "Are you okay if I join them?" And I was like, "I can't think of anyone better to join them." That quartet became Moonstruck, who was the quartet that won in 2014 with my chorus that also won that year. So it was kind of cool that it came full circle that way, yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: That's awesome. We've talked a lot about your journey and your folks. But you also have the experience of singing with your siblings—

speaker: Christina
words: I do.

speaker: Megan
words: —who we've yet to chat about.

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: Tell me a little bit about the quartets that you've sung in with Sam and Josh and what your sibling dynamic kind of looks like in those spaces

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah, for sure. So I've only sung with Joshua officially in Sweet & Sour, and that is a more recent quartet. Samantha and I go way back. [both laugh]

speaker: Megan
words: Waaay back.

speaker: Christina
words: We go way back. We had more opportunities. We didn't— there wasn't a place for mixed quartet singing yet, so Samantha and I sang more together. Our first quartet together was a quartet called Sister Act, and it was comprised of Samantha on tenor, and me on baritone, and sister pairings Andrea and Amanda on lead and bass respectively. And we were all pretty young; we were all around the same age. And this was right after Cloud Nine, I think. So it was around 2012/2013 is when I was in that quartet with Samantha, and it was definitely a learning experience. She was still in high school at the time, and I was just out of college. So it was— we were all just kind— of lives shifting and changing.

And while we were with Sister Act, we were both approached to form another quartet with Katrine Dickau, who was a good family friend of ours, and our mom, and that became Taken For Granite. So we said, "This was a wonderful experience, Sister Act. We love you both very much, but we're going to go and do this now." And they gave their blessing. And then we competed the first time in 2014. We came in third in the same contest that Moonstruck came in first. And then 2015, we came in second by like two points. And then we came in first in 2016 with a sizable difference, which was what I would want to have instead of a really, really, really close contest, which, you know, sometimes that happens too, and the win is still worth it, [laughs] but it was good to feel that we deserved it and that it was just a good reward there. So that was amazing, an amazing experience. And I'm excited to see where High Gear goes from this point too. But that's Taken For Granite, and then we're still technically active even though we don't rehearse. But then Samantha and I started Sweet & Sour with our brother and then Mert, and since then we've had to take a break because Samantha's with GQ. So yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: Hard life.

speaker: Christina
words: I know. [laughs] Wow! Pretty exciting for her though.

speaker: Megan
words: Yeah.

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: You mentioned the "Everyone in Harmony" initiative as, you know, having this impact on, you know, where you get to sing and who you get to sing with. Can you tell us, tell me a little bit more about kind of like what that meant for you and for your family and like all of that?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah. So I've been a fan of the Barbershop Harmony Society when it was still SPEBSQUA [Society for the Preservation and Encouragement of Barber Shop Quartet Singing in America]. And I used to watch the contest DVDs like I would a regular movie at home. Like these people were celebrities to me because growing up that's the content I had. And I—

speaker: Megan
words: "American Idol" who?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah, exactly. I want to be like that quartet. So I definitely fell in love with BHS and with that organization just in a whole. And I always wondered, I— not even! I just, I had a feeling that I probably never will be able to sing in that organization because it's for the boys and I'm not a boy. I even, in like middle school, cause I used to go to the Granite Statesmen rehearsals all. The. time and would just hang out with the guys, and we would sing tags at the breaks and afterwards and I would go to afterglow with them, and I would sing their songs with them too in baritone in their key. Like I was definitely the barberbrat. And it— I— they wanted to dress me up as a guy and bring me out on stage in a quartet. And I said, "I would love nothing more than to just be that." So I definitely had that thought in my head, even as a kid. But I'm— once they were opening it up and saying everyone can sing, I— it's been a dream come true, truly. Like with the experiences with Sweet & Sour, especially, and making the top 20 a couple times too. It's just like, that was surreal. Just to watch it as a kid and like say that this is my "American Idol," to be part of that contest in that capacity was just, no words can really describe it.

speaker: Megan
words: Yeah. Tell me a little bit about your International Contest experience with Sweet & Sour. What was— you, we were there in what New Orleans...? Where were we?

speaker: Christina
words: We, so.

speaker: Megan
words: Cleveland!

speaker: Christina
words: Yep, we were in Cleveland last. That was, that was 2024, right?

speaker: Megan
words: Mmhmm.

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah, and that's when we came in 16th. Still surreal. Just crazy. Cleveland was fun. We knew it was kind of coming to an end for the time being because Samantha already accepted GQ's invite to sing with them. And we kind of knew that this was going to be our last hoorah for a while. So we went in guns blazing and not caring really because there was no risk. There's nothing like, "This is it for the time being. We'll drop the mic and go." We debuted "Lover Come Back" at that contest, and we were not expecting the room to go as nuts as it did. It's kind of wild. Like, and you can't actually hear it on the recording as well as it was in person. Like in person, it was like, it was shocking.

speaker: Megan
words: I was on my feet. It was crazy.

speaker: Christina
words: It was really fun. It was a— that was a very cool contest to be a part of. The previous year, '23, we made the 20 for the first time. We came in 18th, and that was the year that we had to start the quarterfinals where we were drawn first to sing out of 60 some odd quartets. So it was bright and early morning on that Tuesday that week. And we came out guns blazing. We were like, "Let's set the bar. Let's do it." So I'm glad it paid off, but yeah, it's just been a crazy journey with them. And even from the beginning when we didn't really have a home to compete, cause we were competing in 2018 and 2019 through BHS and actually 2017 as well. We were at the fall contest in 2017 as like— I don't know if MBHA [Mixed Barbershop Harmony Association] was around at that point, but it was, they opened it up to mixed quartets, and we did awful. [laughs] That recording is somewhere, and it is real bad. And then we went to Area One one year as well, which is up in Nova Scotia area, and we competed out of there for MBHA specifically, and that was cool to get those, like, that experience and be a part of that group. But yeah, it's been, it's been a fun journey to see us grow score wise, as well as just as people and as musicians.

speaker: Megan
words: You've also had the opportunity to work with some young singers with Sweet & Sour. Can you tell me a little bit about like sharing your love of barbershop with the next generation and like being a part of that educational space?

speaker: Christina
words: I've been both an attendee and on staff and on faculty — all of the things — for Harmony EXplosion Northeast. [Megan shows camera Harmony EXplosion Northeast shirt] Yep. Yep. Repping the shirts here.

speaker: Megan
words: Shameless promotion.

speaker: Christina
words: I attended as a kid, and I kind of got grandfathered in. And this happened a lot when I was a kid of like, camps that were only for high schoolers, but I was younger, but I was already a barbershopper, so like the people in charge were like, "Ah, you can do it." So I was— a lot of the time I was the youngest person in the room, but I didn't mind cause I had the knowledge already. And I just, I love sharing it with people, especially young people and especially like spreading the word and not necessarily pushing them to join an organization per se, just to sing barbershop and just have fun and learn new things. And I think that's why tags are great. Cause you can just pull it out real quick and teach it to anyone. And I think especially with younger people, they're sponges, and they just latch on immediately, and it just makes the experience even more exciting. I love the experience of seeing someone sing in a quartet for the first time and have the chords ring around them if they're just posting or even if they're singing a different part and like. Their eyes get wide and it's like, "Ah, you caught the bug and you're in it now." Once you catch it, you can't quit. So that's one of my favorite things to experience. Yeah.

speaker: Megan
words: How many summers were you doing like HXNE as a teen? Like, was that just like a part of your routine?

speaker: Christina
words: Yeah. It was every summer, basically until I aged out. But even when I aged out, I was invited back as part of a pickup quartet for the first year that I was not eligible to actually be there with Jen Wheaton. And it was Mary Nasto at the time, I don't know her last name now. And is it Morgan Lacroix? It might've been Morgan, I can't remember, It's been so long. That was so many years ago. And then I came back as chorus manager for the women's chorus. So I was kind of there just for the faculty part, I was there for the quartet and whatever they needed, but I was also in the room, so I was there watching the rehearsals all weekend anyway. And Sweet & Sour has also been on faculty as a quartet as well. So it's just, it's very cool to just still be involved.

speaker: Megan
words: Yeah. You're just a part of the fabric of HXNE. It's so great that it is back in the way that it is.
